patterns.pattern: False alarms that drown real cases
patterns.role_note: Dutroux 'X-dossiers' — witness claims of an elite abuse network.
patterns.pattern_summary: False stories about child trafficking take police time and public attention away from real cases. In July 2020 a claim spread online that the furniture company Wayfair was selling children through its listings. The US National Human Trafficking Hotline received hundreds of reports about it within days, and Polaris, the charity that runs the hotline, said the volume made it harder to help people who needed help; none of the reports contained new information. In 2016 a false claim known as "Pizzagate", that a Washington pizza restaurant was the centre of a child-abuse ring, led a man to fire a rifle inside the restaurant. In London, the Metropolitan Police spent more than £2 million on Operation Midland, which investigated claims made by Carl Beech about a ring of powerful men; the claims were false, Beech was jailed for perverting the course of justice, and he had separately admitted child sexual offences. In the 1980s the McMartin preschool case in California, built on claims of ritual abuse, cost about $14 million and ended without a conviction.

cases.title: South Korea — Truth and Reconciliation Commission finds state responsible for overseas-adoption abuses
cases.who: South Korean government; private adoption agencies (Wikipedia list cites Holt Children's Services, Eastern Social Welfare Society, Korea Social Service, Korea Welfare Services)
cases.what: On 26 March 2025, after a two-year inquiry into petitions from 367 adoptees sent abroad between 1964 and 1999 to 11 countries, the commission found human rights violations in at least 56 cases. It found agencies sent set numbers of children each month to meet foreign agencies' demand, falsely registered children with known parents as orphans, did not properly obtain consent and failed to vet adoptive parents. It said the state treated overseas adoption as a cheap alternative to domestic welfare and recommended an official apology and ratification of the Hague Convention. President Lee Jae-myung apologised on 2 October 2025.
cases.cover_up: The commission found the government neglected its duty to oversee agencies; children were falsely registered as orphans and identities were swapped when a child died before departure.

cases.title: Dutroux affair — kidnap, abuse and murder of girls; police and justice failures
cases.who: Marc Dutroux, Michelle Martin, Michel Lelièvre; Belgian Gendarmerie and judicial police
cases.what: Dutroux, on parole for earlier rapes, kidnapped six girls aged 8 to 19 in 1995–96; he was found guilty of kidnapping and raping all six, killing two and causing the deaths of two others. He was arrested in August 1996, and in October 1996 hundreds of thousands of Belgians joined the White March in Brussels to protest police and judicial failures. A parliamentary inquiry chaired by Marc Verwilghen sharply criticised the police investigation. On 22 June 2004 Dutroux was sentenced to life; his ex-wife Michelle Martin got 30 years and Michel Lelièvre 25; businessman Michel Nihoul was acquitted of kidnapping and conspiracy but convicted of drug trafficking and other crimes (five years). Belgium later reorganised its police forces.
cases.cover_up: Dutroux was released early in 1992 from a 13.5-year sentence over prosecutor and psychiatrist objections. Police missed chances, including voices heard in his cellar and unreviewed videotapes; rivalry between Gendarmerie and judicial police hampered the hunt. Judge Connerotte was removed in Oct 1996 for attending a victims' fundraising dinner.

cases.title: Flanders — historical abuse in youth institutions and boarding schools, parliamentary apology
cases.who: Flemish youth institutions, youth centres and boarding schools
cases.what: After clergy abuse cases, further cases emerged of child abuse in Flemish institutions between 1930 and 1990. A working group of experts led by child psychiatrist Peter Adriaenssens, set up by Welfare Minister Jo Vandeurzen, produced two reports recognising the wide scope of abuse. On 23 April 2014 Flemish Parliament Speaker Jan Peumans formally apologised to victims of abuse in boarding schools and youth centres. A temporary recognition and mediation commission set up in 2014 was later made permanent; it received 121 reports in 2024.

cases.title: Adriaenssens commission and Vangheluwe resignation, Belgium
cases.who: Catholic Church in Belgium, about 29 religious orders; Bishop Roger Vangheluwe of Bruges
cases.what: Bishop Roger Vangheluwe of Bruges resigned in April 2010 after admitting he abused his nephew from 1973 to 1986. The church-backed commission led by psychiatrist Peter Adriaenssens received 475 complaints in six months; its report of 10 September 2010 recorded 13 suicides linked to clerical abuse and 102 verified alleged abusers in about 29 orders. In June 2010 police raided church premises and seized the commission's files (Operation Chalice/Kelk); an appeals court later ruled the raids disproportionate.
cases.cover_up: Judicial raid in June 2010 seized the commission's files (later ruled disproportionate); commission members resigned

cases.title: Belgium — Halsberghe commission (2000) and convictions
cases.who: Catholic Church in Belgium
cases.what: A church commission chaired by Godelieve Halsberghe from 2000 received over 300 complaints and upheld 32 of 33 formal ones; 31 were time-barred. Convictions included Fr Bruno Vos (nine years in 2009 for raping four minors), Robert Borremans (five years, 2008) and two Brothers jailed for ten years each in 2005 for abusing disabled people. On 24 June 2010 police raided the archbishop's palace in Mechelen, seizing 450 dossiers, and searched Cardinal Danneels' residence.
cases.cover_up: In about half the 32 upheld cases the accused refused to appear; 31 cases were time-barred and only one reached court; in June 2010 police seized 450 internal dossiers from the Mechelen archbishop's palace

cases.title: Wonderland Club / Operation Cathedral
cases.who: The Wonderland Club (encrypted online network)
cases.what: An international online ring that ran for about four years over encrypted internet chat; each new member had to supply 10,000 images of child abuse. Members held at least 750,000 images and 1,800 videos. Led by the UK National Crime Squad, police in 12 to 13 countries (reported figures differ) acted simultaneously on 2 September 1998, about 1,500 officers raiding 107 homes and making 104 arrests. CNN reported in February 2001 that only 17 of the children in the images had been identified, six of them in Britain. The investigation began after US Customs exposed a related ring, the Orchid Club, in 1996.

cases.title: Fr Eric Dejaeger — Oblate in Nunavut
cases.who: Missionary Oblates of Mary Immaculate; Belgian-born Fr Eric Dejaeger
cases.what: Belgian-born Oblate missionary Eric Dejaeger had served a five-year sentence in the early 1990s for 11 counts of sexual and indecent assault against children in Baker Lake, Nunavut. When charged over Igloolik he fled to Belgium, where he lived in Oblate homes for 16 years despite an international warrant; Oblate officials acknowledged they knew he was about to leave. Returned to Canada in 2011, he was convicted on 12 September 2014 of 24 further counts, and with eight guilty pleas was sentenced in 2015 for 32 sex crimes against Inuit children in Igloolik between 1978 and 1982. He received 19 years (eight after time served); appeals were dismissed in 2018.

cases.title: Kidflix / Operation Stream
cases.who: Kidflix (paid streaming platform, 1.8 million users 2022–2025)
cases.what: Kidflix, created in 2021, let users stream as well as download abuse videos, paying in cryptocurrency converted to tokens; 91,000 unique videos (6,288 hours) were uploaded. German and Dutch authorities seized the server on 11 March 2025, when it held about 72,000 videos. Operation Stream, led by Bavarian police with 38 countries and Europol, identified 1,393 suspects and arrested 79 during action weeks in March 2025; Europol called it the largest child sexual exploitation operation in its history.

cases.title: Operation Cumberland — AI-generated abuse material platform
cases.who: Paid platform distributing AI-generated abuse material (Danish main suspect)
cases.what: A Danish national arrested in November 2024 ran a platform distributing AI-generated abuse material he produced; users paid a symbolic fee for a password. Most arrests came on 26 February 2025 in an operation led by Danish police with 18 other countries; 273 suspects were identified and 25 arrested. Europol called it one of the first cases involving AI-generated CSAM and noted the lack of national laws covering it.

cases.title: Operation Gargamel — Belgian-led investigation of 9 million files
cases.who: Offenders producing their own abuse material
cases.what: Belgian federal judicial police found more than 9 million images and videos, mostly never seen before, in a house search. With Europol victim-identification taskforces, 90 suspects (24 in Belgium) and 110 victims were identified by March 2020; an Australian suspect was sentenced to 15 years. Police in over 40 countries received intelligence packages.

cases.title: Europol sprint on buyers of live-distant abuse in the Philippines (2024)
cases.who: Buyers worldwide directing livestreamed abuse by traffickers in the Philippines
cases.what: From 24 to 28 June 2024, 32 investigators at Europol processed leads from US HSI investigations into networks exploiting children in the Philippines: over 10 million lines of chat between about 12,000 customer accounts and 100 seller accounts, built up over 12 years. The sprint produced information packages that may lead authorities in 24 countries to 197 buyers. Europol notes buyers direct traffickers to abuse children in real time on webcam and some travel to the Philippines to abuse children in person.

cases.title: EU Child Sexual Abuse Regulation ('chat control') and interim derogation
cases.who: European Commission, Council and Parliament
cases.what: The Commission proposed the CSA Regulation (COM(2022) 209) to require platforms to assess risks and allow detection orders; it has been deadlocked over mandatory scanning. The interim derogation from the ePrivacy Directive (Regulation (EU) 2021/1232, in force 2 August 2021, extended in 2024) let providers voluntarily detect abuse material; with no agreement it lapsed on 3 April 2026. A new temporary derogation, Regulation (EU) 2026/1881, was adopted on 24 July 2026 and published 28 July 2026. As of October 2026 the permanent regulation has not been adopted.

cases.title: Dutroux 'X-dossiers' — witness claims of an elite abuse network
cases.who: Witnesses X1–X4 (claims); Belgian prosecutors
cases.what: Witnesses told investigators in 1996–97 of abuse parties and unsolved murders involving Marc Dutroux, Michel Nihoul and prominent people. Prosecutors ultimately dismissed the statements, and investigators were criticised for leading a key witness; an officer charged in 1997 with falsifying her statements was cleared in 1999. In 1999 the Guardian reported renewed cover-up claims, and that the parliamentary inquiry's chair said his findings had been muzzled. The claims of an elite network remain unproven; a 1999 book by three journalists argued the witnesses were more credible than portrayed.

flows.what: South Korean children sent for adoption to Belgium; part of about 163,898 sent abroad 1953–2008. The 2025 Truth and Reconciliation Commission found state-enabled fraud in overseas adoptions.

flows.title: Igloolik (Nunavut) → Belgium: Fr Eric Dejaeger (fugitive 1995–2011)
flows.what: About to be charged in 1995, the Oblate fled to Belgium; Oblate officials acknowledged knowing he was leaving, and he lived 16 years in Oblate houses despite an international warrant until returned in 2011. In 2015 he was sentenced to 19 years for 32 offences against Inuit children in Igloolik (1978–82).

networks.what: The four agencies held guardianship over children and sent them abroad under government policy; Holt sent about half (AP). The TRC (March 2025) found agencies met monthly quotas for foreign partners, falsified orphan status and swapped identities, and that the state failed to supervise them. All four were implicated in the petitions (Guardian, 2023).

networks.what: Paid streaming platform, 1.8 million users (2022–2025), 91,000 videos; 1,393 suspects identified, 79 arrested.

networks.name: Livestreamed abuse of children in the Philippines (OSEC)
networks.what: Not one organisation: thousands of local traffickers, often parents or relatives, paid by foreign buyers to livestream abuse. IJM: 1 in 100 Filipino children affected in 2022.

networks.name: Roman Catholic Church
networks.what: The Holy See governs about 1.3 billion Catholics. From 1922 (and 1962) canonical abuse cases were handled under strict secrecy; from 2001 they were reserved to the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith under pontifical secret, which was lifted in December 2019. National inquiries in Ireland, the US, Australia, Germany, France, the Netherlands, Belgium, Portugal, Spain and elsewhere found bishops moved accused clergy and avoided police. The UN Committee on the Rights of the Child in 2014 found practices that led to impunity.

cases.title: Landslide Productions / Operations Avalanche and Ore
cases.who: Landslide Productions (payment portal, Thomas and Janice Reedy)
cases.what: Landslide, a Fort Worth, Texas portal run by Thomas and Janice Reedy, processed credit-card sign-ups for third-party sites, some offering child abuse images. US agents raided it in August 1999; a jury convicted Thomas Reedy, who was sentenced to 1,335 years (reduced to 180 on appeal), and Janice Reedy got 14 years. US Operation Avalanche examined about 35,000 names on the database, and the FBI passed details of 7,272 British residents to UK police, starting Operation Ore, Britain's biggest computer crime investigation; raids began in May 2002. CEOP said 140 children had been rescued in the UK. Later forensic examination showed large-scale credit card fraud in Landslide's records (54,348 sets of stolen card details), and some people were wrongly accused; a legal challenge in 2009 argued that many convictions for incitement rested on flawed credit-card evidence. Follow-on operations took place in other countries.
cases.cover_up: Later reconstruction of the Landslide data found many listed names were victims of credit-card fraud, and the validity of UK Operation Ore procedures was questioned; an estimated 33 suicides followed in the UK.

cases.title: Sri Lanka — 1980s 'baby farms' supplying intercountry adoption
cases.who: Baby farms, brokers, hospital doctors and nurses acting as intermediaries for Western agencies
cases.what: A Dutch Zembla documentary (September 2017) reported that babies were bought or abducted from hospitals, handed to paid 'acting mothers' and sold for adoption, mainly to the Netherlands, with others to the UK, Sweden and Germany. Sri Lanka's health minister Rajitha Senaratne acknowledged on camera that 'there were a lot of baby farms back then' and announced an inquiry and a DNA databank. Sri Lanka changed its rules after a 1987 police raid found 20 newborns and 22 women held in 'prison like conditions'.
cases.cover_up: Adoption records were widely falsified; 'acting mothers' were paid to pose as birth mothers in court.

cases.title: Switzerland — authorities' irregularities in intercountry adoptions (Sri Lanka, India, Tibet…); proposed ban
cases.who: Swiss federal and cantonal authorities; private adoption agencies
cases.what: Swiss authorities soon realised that the placement of children for adoption, often wrongly presented as orphans, was also driven by economic interests and linked to organised child trafficking; decisions were often made on incomplete or falsified documents, and checks on foster families and on legal requirements were insufficient. From the 2010s, under pressure from groups such as Back to the Roots, intercountry adoptions from Tibet, Sri Lanka and India drew public attention. In 2018 the Federal Assembly commissioned a study on intercountry adoption; the Federal Council acknowledged the authorities' irregularities and omissions in 2020 and 2023, and at the end of 2024 recommended a general ban on intercountry adoption.

cases.title: Switzerland — 'Kinder der Landstrasse': Yenish children removed by Pro Juventute (1926–1973)
cases.who: Pro Juventute foundation, with federal and cantonal authorities
cases.what: From 1926 to 1973 the Pro Juventute foundation's 'Hilfswerk für die Kinder der Landstrasse' (Charity for the Children of the Country Road) took around 600 Yenish children from their families and forcibly placed them in homes or foster families; around 2,000 children of the Swiss Traveller community are believed to have been affected by such measures overall. The persecution depended on authorities at every level of government, which were closely intertwined with Pro Juventute in personnel and co-funded the Hilfswerk. On 20 February 2025 the Swiss government, taking note of a legal opinion led by Professor Oliver Diggelmann, acknowledged that the persecution of Yenish and Sinti people was a crime against humanity under current international law (but not a 'cultural genocide'), and reaffirmed its apology. (Care agent covers Verdingkinder.)

cases.title: Swiss administrative detention and forced placements (incl. Verdingkinder)
cases.who: Swiss cantonal and municipal authorities; about 650 institutions
cases.what: The Independent Expert Commission on Administrative Detention, set up under the Federal Act of 21 March 2014, presented its final report on 2 September 2019. It found more than 60,000 people were interned in about 650 institutions without court order, mainly from 1930 to 1981, and that victims were abused physically, psychologically and sexually. The Swiss government had apologised in 2010; a 2016 law created a CHF 25,000 'solidarity contribution' for victims of compulsory measures, including children placed as indentured farm labourers (Verdingkinder).

cases.title: University of Zurich pilot study — Catholic Church in Switzerland
cases.who: Swiss Bishops' Conference and religious orders (commissioned study)
cases.what: Historians at the University of Zurich, led by Monika Dommann and Marietta Meier and commissioned by the Swiss Bishops' Conference and religious orders, published a pilot study in September 2023 on sexual abuse in the Swiss Catholic Church since the mid-20th century. They documented 1,002 cases involving 510 accused people and 921 victims; 74% of the documents concerned abuse of minors. More than half the cases occurred in pastoral work and about 30% in Catholic children's homes, schools and boarding schools. The researchers called the cases 'the tip of the iceberg' and found that church criminal law was hardly ever applied, with many cases kept secret, covered up or trivialised.

cases.what: An invitation-only bulletin board, used by an estimated 600 people, whose applicants had to upload abuse material of children aged 12 or under and keep uploading to stay. NBC reported the computers hosting the site were in Georgia, US, and the top administrators were in France and Canada. In August 2011 Attorney General Eric Holder and DHS Secretary Janet Napolitano announced charges against 72 people, with arrests on five continents including 43 in the US. By January 2013, 57 had been arrested, 45 had pleaded guilty and one was convicted at trial; 42 had been sentenced to between 10 years and life. Fifteen were known only by online identities. DOJ said at least 38 children were being abused by group members.

Charged in Fribourg with human trafficking, encouraging prostitution, sexual acts with children and abuse material, he was sentenced by a Swiss court on 1 March 2018 to 16 years.

networks.name: Roman Catholic Church
networks.what: The Holy See governs about 1.3 billion Catholics. From 1922 (and 1962) canonical abuse cases were handled under strict secrecy; from 2001 they were reserved to the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith under pontifical secret, which was lifted in December 2019. patterns.pattern: Moved instead of stopped
patterns.role_note: Romania–UK 'loverboy' network dismantled — 21 arrested (Eurojust, 2020).
patterns.pattern_summary: When a priest, religious brother, teacher or head teacher was found to be abusing children, the institution they worked for often moved them instead of reporting them to the police. The move was to another parish, another school, another state or another country, and the person went on working with children. A Pennsylvania grand jury reported in 2018 that bishops in six dioceses had moved priests they knew to be abusers. In Australia, Bishop Mulkearns knew by late 1975 that the priest Gerald Ridsdale was abusing children and kept appointing him to new parishes. In Melbourne in 2008, the Adass Israel School paid for its head teacher, Malka Leifer, to fly to Israel before the police were told of the allegations against her. In England, an internal report in 1982 described how the barrister John Smyth had beaten boys he met through evangelical holiday camps; he moved to Zimbabwe in 1984, the police were not told until 2013, and a 2024 review called him "a problem solved and exported to Africa". The map draws 34 documented moves and colors the countries that sent or received an abuser.

patterns.pattern: The adoption pipeline that keeps moving
patterns.role: Sending country, later closed or suspended
patterns.role_note: 1990: hold: Romania puts a hold on international adoptions (July) after 'babies-for-export' anger 1991: halt: Romania halts adoptions (June 1991) and outlaws baby selling (August 1991) 2001: moratorium: Romania imposes temporary ban on intercountry adoption; government commission finds funds siphoned by middlemen and officials 2004: ban: Romania's June 2004 law bans foreign adoption except by grandparents (under EU pressure)
patterns.pattern_summary: Intercountry adoption is the adoption of a child from one country by parents in another. From the 1950s onward the children came from a series of countries in turn. South Korea sent about 164,000 children abroad between 1953 and 2008. Later the main sources included Romania in the 1990s, Guatemala until 2008, Cambodia, Vietnam, Nepal and Ethiopia. In each of these, investigations found children who had been bought, taken from their families or falsely registered as orphans, and adoptions were stopped or suspended by the sending country, the receiving countries, or both. In 2025 South Korea's Truth and Reconciliation Commission found the state responsible for human rights violations in its overseas adoptions. Receiving countries also began to investigate: the Netherlands suspended all intercountry adoption in 2021 after a government committee reported abuses, and China ended the practice in 2024. The map draws 59 documented adoption flows and marks which sending countries were later closed or suspended.

patterns.pattern: Platforms, servers and the money behind them
patterns.role: Hosts the most reported abuse material (IWF 2025)
patterns.role_note: 21,188 web addresses actioned by the IWF in 2025 (7% of the total).
patterns.pattern_summary: Online abuse of children depends on ordinary businesses: companies that host websites, apps and social platforms, payment services and banks. In 2025 the Internet Watch Foundation, a British charity that finds and removes abuse images, found most of the material it removed on servers in Bulgaria, the United States, the Netherlands, Romania and France. Reports of suspected abuse to the US CyberTipline, most of them made by American technology companies, rose from 4,560 in 1998 to more than 36 million in 2023, then fell to about 20.5 million in 2024; the centre that runs it attributed part of the fall to Meta encrypting its messages. Money for watching abuse streamed live flows from Australia, Britain, the United States and other wealthy countries to the Philippines. In 2020 the Australian bank Westpac agreed to pay a A$1.3 billion penalty for breaches of money-laundering law that included failing to check payments that could be linked to child exploitation. The classified advertising site Backpage earned more than $500 million from advertisements, including ones used to sell children, before US authorities shut it down in 2018.

patterns.pattern: Officials who took part or looked away
patterns.role_note: Romania — post-1989 adoption trade and 2004 ban; Romanian state orphanages under Ceaușescu and after 1989; Romania — girls in state institutions at risk; victims sent across Europe (US TIP 2025).
patterns.pattern_summary: In 238 cases on this map, police officers, prosecutors, judges, politicians, civil servants, soldiers or intelligence officers took part in the abuse, or a court or inquiry found that they ignored, concealed or obstructed it. In Rotherham, in the north of England, an independent inquiry in 2014 estimated that about 1,400 children had been sexually exploited between 1997 and 2013 and called the failures of the council and the police "blatant"; three earlier reports had been suppressed or ignored. In Australia in 1972, a senior police officer offered a detective a promotion to stop investigating a monsignor. In North Wales, the police investigated allegations against their own officers. In Mexico, after the journalist Lydia Cacho exposed an abuse ring in Cancún, Puebla state police arrested her in 2005, and leaked phone calls recorded the state governor discussing her detention; he was arrested in 2021 on torture charges.

cases.title: Project Spade — Azov Films, Toronto
cases.who: Azov Films (Toronto distributor of 'naturist' films of children)
cases.what: Toronto police undercover officers made contact with a man sharing graphic abuse images in October 2010, which led to Azov Films, a Toronto company run by Brian Way that produced and sold films of child exploitation worldwide; after a joint investigation with the US Postal Inspection Service, police raided the business. Police said it was a $4 million business distributing to over 50 countries and seized over 45 terabytes of data. On 14 November 2013 Toronto police announced 348 arrests and 386 children rescued; those arrested included 40 school teachers, nine doctors and nurses, six law enforcement personnel, nine pastors and priests and three foster parents. Way was arrested in 2011 and in 2016 was found guilty of making and distributing child sexual abuse material and sentenced to ten years, reduced after a judge found he had been abused in jail.
cases.cover_up: Germany's BKA received the customer list in October 2011 but began investigating only in October 2012; a German MP on the list later resigned, and information about the case was passed to his party leader.

cases.title: Romania — post-1989 adoption trade and 2004 ban
cases.who: Private adoption agencies and intermediaries; Romanian authorities
cases.what: After Ceaușescu's fall, television images of about 100,000 children in orphanages led to an adoption boom; private agencies charged €7,500–25,000 and the system 'quickly became awash in corruption' (DW). Romania halted adoptions in June 1991 and, under EU pressure, passed a law in June 2004 banning all foreign adoptions except by grandparents. The European Parliament's rapporteur Baroness Emma Nicholson had criticised 'international adoption and child trafficking' in Romania. Romania's own HCCH return shows 458 intercountry adoptions in 2002, 332 in 2003, 2 in 2005 and 0 in 2006.

cases.title: Romanian state orphanages under Ceaușescu and after 1989
cases.who: Romanian state orphanages and institutions for disabled children
cases.what: Decree 770 (1966) banned abortion, and many children born afterwards were abandoned in state institutions, where they suffered neglect, physical and sexual abuse and sedation; physical and sexual abuse was reported to be common at the Siret children's psychiatric hospital. After 1989 large numbers of children were adopted abroad amid corruption and irregularities, and in 2004, under EU pressure, Romania banned international adoption except by grandparents. A 2009 BBC investigation found poor conditions persisted in some institutions.

cases.title: Bosnia — trafficking of women and girls; IPTF monitors and SFOR/DynCorp contractors
cases.who: Traffickers and bar owners; local Bosnian police; UN International Police Task Force (IPTF) monitors; US SFOR civilian contractors (DynCorp)
cases.what: Human Rights Watch's November 2002 report 'Hopes Betrayed' documented women and girls trafficked mostly from Moldova, Romania and Ukraine into post-war Bosnia and held in debt bondage in bars and brothels. Local police were found acting as owners, guards and clients; 18 IPTF monitors who purchased women, visited brothels or faced trafficking-related charges went home, and none was confirmed prosecuted. A US Army CID report documented DynCorp contractors buying women from brothels; one confessed to buying a woman (with an Uzi) for 1,600 Deutschmarks. On 2 August 2002 a British employment tribunal unanimously found DynCorp had unfairly dismissed IPTF monitor Kathryn Bolkovac after she reported the trafficking.
cases.cover_up: Immunity: IPTF monitors were repatriated rather than prosecuted (18 returned home; HRW found no prosecution by Nov 2002); DynCorp contractors were sent home, preventing their use as witnesses; DynCorp fired whistleblower Kathryn Bolkovac in April 2001.

cases.title: Kosovo — trafficking for forced prostitution and the international presence (Amnesty 2004)
cases.who: Criminal networks; demand from NATO KFOR soldiers, UN police and international staff
cases.what: Amnesty International's May 2004 report said Kosovo had become a major destination for women and girls trafficked for forced prostitution since NATO troops and UN administrators arrived in 1999, with the international presence generating 80% of traffickers' income at the time. Women and girls were brought mainly from Moldova, Romania, Ukraine and Russia via Serbia, and local girls were also abducted. The UN peacekeeping department acknowledged in 2004 that peacekeepers had 'come to be seen as part of the problem in trafficking rather than the solution'.
cases.cover_up: Amnesty found no evidence of criminal proceedings against any military personnel in their home countries.

cases.title: Romania — girls in state institutions at risk; victims sent across Europe (US TIP 2025)
cases.who: Traffickers; staff of some government-run institutions
cases.what: The 2025 US TIP report says most identified victims are women and girls exploited in Romania and in Austria, France, Germany, Italy, Spain and the UK; children in government-run institutions, particularly girls in homes for persons with disabilities, are at risk of sex trafficking; and Roma children as young as 11 are 'sold' into marriage. Courts convicted 161 traffickers (143 for sex trafficking) and 600 victims were identified in 2024.
cases.cover_up: Alleged complicity, misconduct and negligence by government employees in cases involving children in government-run homes remained a concern.

cases.title: 764 network — founder sentenced to 80 years
cases.who: 764 (online network on Discord/Telegram; founder Bradley Cadenhead)
cases.what: 764, named after the first digits of the ZIP code of Stephenville, Texas, extorted minors into producing abuse material, self-harm and animal cruelty. Its founder, Bradley Cadenhead, was arrested in August 2021 aged 16 and on 16 May 2023 was sentenced in Texas to 80 years after pleading guilty to nine counts of possession/promotion of child sexual abuse material. The US DOJ describes 764 as a nihilistic violent extremist network and its Counterterrorism Section prosecutes it; on 29 April 2025 DOJ announced the arrests of two alleged leaders of the subgroup '764 Inferno', in North Carolina and in Greece. On 10 December 2025 Canada became the first country to list 764 as a terrorist entity.

cases.title: Romania — former Bishop of Huși jailed for raping a seminary pupil
cases.who: Romanian Orthodox Church, Diocese of Huși; Huși Orthodox Theological Seminary
cases.what: Romania's High Court of Cassation and Justice upheld a Galați Court of Appeal ruling sentencing former Bishop Corneliu Bârlădeanu (Cornel Onilă) to eight years for rape and other sexual assaults, in a case that began with 2017 recordings allegedly showing him with a minor pupil of the Huși seminary. Former archimandrite Sebastian Jitaru received 14 years 2 months for rape and sexual assaults. The diocese and seminary were ordered to pay court costs; the diocese apologised to the victims. Bârlădeanu resigned in August 2017. Media described him as the first senior Romanian Orthodox hierarch to go to prison.
cases.cover_up: The case surfaced in June 2017 when the bishop himself complained to anti-corruption prosecutors that three priests were blackmailing him with a recording; a former archimandrite was earlier jailed for that blackmail.

cases.title: Kidflix / Operation Stream
cases.who: Kidflix (paid streaming platform, 1.8 million users 2022–2025)
cases.what: Kidflix, created in 2021, let users stream as well as download abuse videos, paying in cryptocurrency converted to tokens; 91,000 unique videos (6,288 hours) were uploaded. German and Dutch authorities seized the server on 11 March 2025, when it held about 72,000 videos. Operation Stream, led by Bavarian police with 38 countries and Europol, identified 1,393 suspects and arrested 79 during action weeks in March 2025; Europol called it the largest child sexual exploitation operation in its history.

cases.title: Romania–UK 'loverboy' network dismantled — 21 arrested (Eurojust, 2020)
cases.who: Romanian organized criminal group using the 'loverboy' method
cases.what: On 9 September 2020 a Romanian–UK Joint Investigation Team supported by Eurojust arrested 21 members of a hierarchical group active since 2009 that seduced vulnerable Romanian girls with false promises of relationships, exploited minors in prostitution in Romania until they turned 18, and then moved them to the UK, Ireland and Germany. Thirty-two house searches were carried out (23 in Romania, 9 in the UK). Eurojust said Romania and the UK had cooperated in 76 trafficking investigations in four years.

cases.title: Galați/Brăila — 'loverboy' ring exploiting minors in Western Europe (2021)
cases.who: Four suspects detained by DIICOT/BCCO
cases.what: In February 2021 Romanian organised-crime police and DIICOT prosecutors searched eight addresses in Galați and Brăila and detained four suspects for human trafficking, trafficking of minors and pimping. Investigators said that from August 2013 the group recruited girls and young women by the 'loverboy' method, hid minors in intermediate lodgings until they turned 18, then exploited them in Western Europe, earning about €350,000; nine victims, minor and adult, had been identified.

patterns.pattern: Governments that took children
patterns.role_note: Argentina — junta's 'systematic plan' to appropriate babies (2012 verdict). Argentina — Abuelas de Plaza de Mayo: 140 stolen grandchildren identified.
patterns.pattern_summary: Some of the largest removals of children from their families were carried out by governments as a matter of policy. Canada, Australia and the United States removed Indigenous children from their families and placed them in residential schools or with non-Indigenous families. In 1951 Denmark sent a group of Greenlandic children to live with Danish families, and France moved children from the island of Réunion to rural France. Since 2022 Russia has deported children from occupied parts of Ukraine; in March 2023 the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for President Vladimir Putin and Maria Lvova-Belova over these deportations.

cases.title: Uruguay — Gelman v. Uruguay: baby taken from disappeared mother (Operation Condor)
cases.who: Uruguayan Defense Information Service (SID); joint Argentine–Uruguayan commando under Operation Condor
cases.what: A pregnant 19-year-old Argentine detained in Buenos Aires in August 1976 was moved secretly to Montevideo, gave birth in a military hospital, and her baby was taken in December 1976 and left with a police officer's family, who raised her under another identity for 23 years. On 24 February 2011 the Inter-American Court of Human Rights found Uruguay responsible for enforced disappearance and suppression of the child's identity, and ruled the 1986 Expiry Law amnesty legally ineffective.
cases.cover_up: Uruguay's 1986 Expiry Law was used to close the investigation in 2003.

cases.title: Argentina — junta's 'systematic plan' to appropriate babies (2012 verdict)
cases.who: Argentine military junta; armed forces and security forces; ESMA
cases.what: On 5 July 2012 Federal Oral Criminal Tribunal No. 6 of Buenos Aires found that the military junta had run a systematic plan to abduct children born to detained or disappeared mothers, between 1976 and 1983. Former dictator Jorge Videla was sentenced to 50 years and the last dictator, Reynaldo Bignone, to 15 years; nine other defendants received 15 to 40 years (MercoPress). The trial covered about 31–35 abductions. The tribunal convicted Bignone of crimes against humanity for implementing the plan.
cases.cover_up: Children's original identities were hidden and they were registered as the biological children of military families and regime allies.

cases.title: Marita Verón case — Tucumán brothel network
cases.who: Brothel and trafficking ring in Tucumán province
cases.what: Marita Verón, aged 23, disappeared in Tucumán in 2002, allegedly abducted into forced prostitution. In December 2012 a Tucumán court acquitted all 13 defendants, provoking national protests and calls to impeach the judges. In December 2013 Tucumán's Supreme Court reversed the acquittals and found 10 of the 13 guilty. Her mother's foundation, created in 2008, says it has helped free hundreds of women and girls from brothels. (Verón was an adult; the case is included because it exposed the national network that also trafficked minors.)
cases.cover_up: Campaigners and the victim's family's lawyers said police were often paid to protect prostitution rings; trial court acquitted all 13 in 2012.

cases.title: Argentina — Abuelas de Plaza de Mayo: 140 stolen grandchildren identified
cases.who: Argentine military regime (1976–83); military families and regime allies who received children
cases.what: The Grandmothers of Plaza de Mayo were founded in 1977 to find children kidnapped with their disappeared parents or born to mothers in detention, who were passed for adoption to military families and regime allies. Their work led to the creation of Argentina's National Bank of Genetic Data. On 7 July 2025 they announced the 140th grandchild identified: a man born on 17 April 1977 at the clandestine centre 'La Escuelita' in Bahía Blanca after his parents were kidnapped in Cutral Có, Neuquén. The Grandmothers had found 97 grandchildren by 2008 and 133 by July 2023.
cases.cover_up: Children were illegally adopted with their original identities hidden; many did not know they were adopted.
cases.network: Argentine military junta — systematic appropriation of children (with Operation Condor partners)

cases.title: Wonderland Club / Operation Cathedral
cases.who: The Wonderland Club (encrypted online network)
cases.what: An international online ring that ran for about four years over encrypted internet chat; each new member had to supply 10,000 images of child abuse. Members held at least 750,000 images and 1,800 videos. Led by the UK National Crime Squad, police in 12 to 13 countries (reported figures differ) acted simultaneously on 2 September 1998, about 1,500 officers raiding 107 homes and making 104 arrests. CNN reported in February 2001 that only 17 of the children in the images had been identified, six of them in Britain. The investigation began after US Customs exposed a related ring, the Orchid Club, in 1996.

cases.title: Próvolo Institute, Luján de Cuyo (Mendoza) — convictions 2019
cases.who: Provolo Institute for the Deaf (Argentina branch); Fr Nicola Corradi, Fr Horacio Corbacho, gardener Armando Gómez; Sr Kumiko Kosaka charged
cases.what: Priests Nicola Corradi (Italian) and Horacio Corbacho and other staff of the Provolo school for deaf children in Luján de Cuyo, Mendoza were arrested in 2016, charged with abusing at least two dozen students. On 25 November 2019 a Mendoza court convicted Corradi, Corbacho and gardener Armando Gómez of abusing children at the school between 2004 and 2016; the victims in the trial were 10 former students. Corradi was sentenced to 42 years, Corbacho to 45 and Gómez to 18. Nun Kumiko Kosaka was charged in 2017 with helping the abuse and with physically abusing students.
cases.cover_up: Corradi had been accused in Verona in 2009 yet continued at the Argentine school; Japanese nun Kumiko Kosaka charged with abuse and covering up

cases.title: Bishop Gustavo Zanchetta of Orán — convicted 2022
cases.who: Diocese of Orán; Bishop Gustavo Zanchetta
cases.what: Bishop Gustavo Zanchetta resigned from the Diocese of Orán in August 2017, citing health, after complaints from clergy, and in December 2017 Pope Francis gave him a post created for him at the Vatican's patrimony office (APSA). Clergy had complained to the nunciature in 2015–2016 about his behaviour with seminarians and explicit images on his phone. On 4 March 2022 a court in Salta sentenced him to four and a half years for continued sexual abuse of two former seminarians, aggravated by his being a minister of religion. Included as a case of a bishop moved to the Vatican, though the victims were adults.
cases.cover_up: After resigning in 2017 amid complaints he was given a post at the Vatican's APSA in December 2017; suspended in January 2019

cases.title: Paraguay — Fr Carlos Urrutigoity and the removal of Bishop Livieres
cases.who: Diocese of Ciudad del Este
cases.what: Argentine priest Carlos Urrutigoity was accused in 2002 in the US of sleeping with boarding-school students, giving them alcohol and sexually abusing a recently graduated seminarian. He then moved to the Diocese of Ciudad del Este, Paraguay, and became its second-in-command in 2014. His case reportedly cost Bishop Livieres his post when Pope Francis removed him in 2014. He was moved back to Mendoza, Argentina, in June 2015. He has not been convicted.
cases.cover_up: After accusations in the US (a 2002 complaint over students at St Gregory's Academy in the Diocese of Scranton), he moved with his group to Ciudad del Este, where Bishop Rogelio Livieres made him vicar general in 2014. Pope Francis removed Livieres in 2014; Urrutigoity left in June 2015. La Nación reported at least five Argentine priests accused of abuse or crimes against humanity had sheltered in Paraguay.

cases.title: Argentina raids on The Family (Children of God) communes

cases.what: On 1 September 1993 Judge Roberto Marquevich ordered raids on Family communes near Buenos Aires; 137 children were taken into state custody and about 30 members arrested. The judge said nine children showed signs of 'cruel and atrocious maltreatment', which the group disputed. Children were later released after examination and no convictions resulted. Raids in Australia (1992, including Panton Hill, Victoria), France and Spain also ended without convictions.

patterns.role_note: Melbourne → Israel (Malka Leifer flown out by her school).
patterns.pattern_summary: When a priest, religious brother, teacher or head teacher was found to be abusing children, the institution they worked for often moved them instead of reporting them to the police. The move was to another parish, another school, another state or another country, and the person went on working with children. A Pennsylvania grand jury reported in 2018 that bishops in six dioceses had moved priests they knew to be abusers. In Australia, Bishop Mulkearns knew by late 1975 that the priest Gerald Ridsdale was abusing children and kept appointing him to new parishes. In Melbourne in 2008, the Adass Israel School paid for its head teacher, Malka Leifer, to fly to Israel before the police were told of the allegations against her. In England, an internal report in 1982 described how the barrister John Smyth had beaten boys he met through evangelical holiday camps; he moved to Zimbabwe in 1984, the police were not told until 2013, and a 2024 review called him "a problem solved and exported to Africa". The map draws 34 documented moves and colors the countries that sent or received an abuser.

patterns.pattern: States that shielded their own
patterns.role_note: Malka Leifer (2014): Extradited January 2021; convicted 3 April 2023; Litzman took a plea deal for breach of trust and resigned from the Knesset (2022)
patterns.pattern_summary: When a person accused of abusing a child is a soldier, a diplomat or a foreign citizen, whether they are tried depends on their own government. UN peacekeepers can be prosecuted only by the country that sent them. In Haiti, a UN investigation found that at least 134 Sri Lankan peacekeepers had sexually exploited and abused at least nine children between 2004 and 2007; 114 were sent home, and none was jailed in Sri Lanka. In 2013 the Vatican recalled its ambassador to the Dominican Republic, Archbishop Józef Wesołowski, while Dominican authorities were investigating him for abusing children, and later told Polish prosecutors that Vatican law did not allow him to be extradited. In 2020 a court in Seoul refused a US request to extradite Son Jong-woo, who had run the abuse website Welcome to Video. In 2013 Morocco's king pardoned Daniel Galván, a Spanish man convicted of raping children, as a gesture towards Spain. In Israel, a deputy health minister interfered with psychiatric assessments of Malka Leifer, which delayed her extradition to Australia for several years.

patterns.pattern: The adoption pipeline that keeps moving
patterns.role_note: 1 documented adoption flows into Israel on this map.

patterns.pattern: Governments that took children
patterns.role_note: Israel — Yemenite, Mizrahi and Balkan children affair.
patterns.pattern_summary: Some of the largest removals of children from their families were carried out by governments as a matter of policy. During Argentina's military dictatorship from 1976 to 1983, about 500 babies were taken from mothers held in detention and given to other families; in 2012 a court found this had been a "systematic plan", and by July 2025, 140 of those children had been identified. Under Franco's dictatorship in Spain, children were taken from Republican mothers and later from unmarried mothers. Canada, Australia and the United States removed Indigenous children from their families and placed them in residential schools or with non-Indigenous families. In 1951 Denmark sent a group of Greenlandic children to live with Danish families, and France moved children from the island of Réunion to rural France. Since 2022 Russia has deported children from occupied parts of Ukraine; in March 2023 the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for President Vladimir Putin and Maria Lvova-Belova over these deportations.

cases.title: Israel/Gaza — UN COI findings on sexual violence incl. against Palestinian boys and on 7 October

cases.what: The UN Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory and Israel found in June 2024 that Israeli security forces subjected Palestinians to sexual and gender-based violence including forced public nudity and sexualised torture, and that 'men and boys were targeted in particular ways'; it found gender persecution of Palestinian men and boys as a crime against humanity. cases.title: Malka Leifer — Adass Israel School, Melbourne
cases.who: Adass Israel School (ultra-Orthodox community school)
cases.what: Headmistress Malka Leifer abused pupils at Melbourne's ultra-Orthodox Adass Israel School between about 2003 and 2007. The school flew her to Israel in March 2008. Australia issued a warrant in 2014 for 74 offences involving at least eight pupils; she was arrested in Israel in August 2014, found in 2019 to have faked mental illness, and extradited on 25 January 2021. On 3 April 2023 a Melbourne jury found her guilty of 18 charges including rape, and in August 2023 she was sentenced to 15 years. In 2015 the Supreme Court of Victoria had ordered the school and Leifer to pay a former pupil about AU$1.27 million.
cases.cover_up: In March 2008, after a teacher confronted her, the school arranged and paid for a 1:20 a.m. flight to Israel for Leifer and four of her children without telling police. cases.title: Yaakov Litzman — breach of trust for shielding Malka Leifer
cases.who: Israeli Ministry of Health; ultra-Orthodox Agudat Yisrael party
cases.what: Former Israeli health minister Yaakov Litzman signed a plea deal in January 2022 admitting breach of trust for pressuring Health Ministry employees to change psychiatric evaluations so that Malka Leifer would appear unfit to stand extradition trial. He resigned from the Knesset in June 2022 and on 8 August 2022 the Jerusalem Magistrate's Court sentenced him to eight months' probation and a fine of about US$900. cases.cover_up: A government minister pressured ministry psychiatrists to alter evaluations of an extradition suspect.

cases.title: Israel — Yemenite, Mizrahi and Balkan children affair
cases.who: Israeli state health and immigration institutions
cases.what: More than 1,000 families, mostly immigrants from Yemen but also dozens from the Balkans, North Africa and other Middle Eastern countries, say babies taken to hospitals in Israel's early years disappeared after parents were told they had died; many believe they were given away for adoption. Three government inquiries since the 1960s concluded that most of the children died of disease and were buried without their parents being informed. In 2016 the government decided to put most of the inquiries' archives online. On 22 February 2021 the government expressed regret and approved a NIS 162 million compensation plan: NIS 150,000 for each child whose death was reported to the family at the time and NIS 200,000 for each child whose fate is unknown.

cases.title: Romania — post-1989 adoption trade and 2004 ban
cases.who: Private adoption agencies and intermediaries; Romanian authorities
cases.what: After Ceaușescu's fall, television images of about 100,000 children in orphanages led to an adoption boom; private agencies charged €7,500–25,000 and the system 'quickly became awash in corruption' (DW). Other claims circulate, including that Ghislaine Maxwell's father Robert Maxwell worked for Israeli intelligence and about Epstein's business ties to former Israeli PM Ehud Barak, who denies wrongdoing. No official body has found that Epstein worked for any intelligence service.

cases.title: Matthew Falder — dark web 'hurtcore' blackmailer
cases.who: Individual offender posting on hurtcore dark web sites
cases.what: A Cambridge-educated Birmingham university researcher posed online as a depressed female artist to lure victims, some as young as 14, into sending images, then blackmailed them into sending increasingly degrading material, which he shared on dark web 'hurtcore' sites. The NCA estimated more than 50 victims between 2009 and 2017. A taskforce of the NCA, GCHQ, US Homeland Security Investigations, the Australian Federal Police and Europol, with police in Israel and Slovenia, identified him after four years; he was arrested in June 2017. He admitted 137 of 188 charges and was jailed for 32 years in February 2018, thought to be the first UK prosecution related to hurtcore material; in October 2018 the Court of Appeal reduced the sentence to 25 years.

patterns.pattern: Where nobody is counting
patterns.role: No national inquiry into institutional abuse found
patterns.role_note: Largest Catholic population in the world; cases surfaced through individual prosecutions and a 2010 parliamentary hearing on one priest
patterns.pattern_summary: Most counts of child abuse and trafficking come from three sources, and each leaves large parts of the world out. The first is surveys that ask a representative sample of people about their experiences. Childlight, a research centre that combines such surveys into global estimates, had them from only 60 countries in its 2026 update, too few to represent South Asia, West and Central Africa, or the Middle East and North Africa. The second is official statistics that governments send to the UN; its 2024 global report on trafficking covered 156 countries, but only 72 supplied figures for 2023. The third is reports from technology companies to the US CyberTipline; in 2025, 14 percent of its 23.4 million reports could not be assigned to any country, and North Korea had 12, a number that reflects how few people there can use American apps. The research for this map also found no national inquiry into abuse in institutions in Italy, Brazil, the Philippines or India.

cases.title: Netherlands — Joustra committee: state failed to stop intercountry adoption abuses; all adoptions suspended
cases.who: Dutch government (Justice ministry), licensed Dutch adoption intermediaries, intermediaries in sending countries
cases.what: The Commission of Inquiry into Intercountry Adoption, set up in 2019 and chaired by Tjibbe Joustra, reported in February 2021 after a two-year investigation that found 'serious violations' in adoptions from countries including Sri Lanka, Indonesia, Bangladesh, Brazil and Colombia between 1967 and 1997/98, and concluded the Dutch government had for decades failed to prevent abuses and protect children's rights. The government suspended all intercountry adoptions with immediate effect on 8 February 2021. About 4,000 of the children were from Sri Lanka.
cases.cover_up: The government revealed in February 2021 that its officials were aware of wrongdoing for years and had failed to intervene (BBC).

The 2025 US TIP report says taxi drivers and hotel, bar and nightclub staff in coastal tourist destinations facilitate child sex trafficking, and cites a study suggesting up to 16 per cent of girls aged 14–17 in one northeastern metropolitan area were likely victims of commercial sexual exploitation.
cases.cover_up: US TIP 2025: no investigations of complicit officials reported; a 2016 child sex-trafficking case involving an elected official in Paraná unresolved.

The order followed the death in July 2026 of a 13-year-old girl in central-western Brazil who, authorities said, was encouraged during a Discord livestream to take her own life. Five teenagers were arrested in connection with her death, and police said the investigation also led them to another girl at risk, whom they reached in time. These totals cover all the issues they lobbied on, not only this one. Where the deadlines were lifted anyway, many institutions filed for bankruptcy. From 2004 to 2025, 40 US Catholic dioceses and religious orders did so, several of them hours or days before a trial, a deposition or a new law took effect. cases.title: Johnny Kitagawa — Johnny & Associates talent agency

The company admitted the abuse in September 2023, split into a new talent agency (Starto Entertainment) and Smile-Up, which handles compensation through a relief committee of three former judges. The BBC documentary 'Predator' (March 2023) and a former trainee's public allegations in April 2023 triggered the reckoning. cases.title: Japan — Bishops' Conference survey: 16 cases
cases.who: Catholic Bishops' Conference of Japan (16 dioceses)
cases.what: The Catholic Bishops' Conference of Japan began a survey of all 16 dioceses in May 2019 and published it on 7 April 2020. It found 16 cases of sexual abuse of minors from the 1950s to the 2010s, called 'the tip of the iceberg'. Most victims took 10 to 30 years to report, some 50 to 70 years. Of the accused, seven were Japanese priests and eight religious or missionaries, seven of them foreign. Earlier internal surveys (2002, 2012) had found two and five cases.
cases.cover_up: Eight accused clerics were transferred; some punished clerics kept working or moved to another diocese; five remained priests. Only one denied case was examined by a third-party panel.

cases.title: Japan — Yomiuri survey of sexual misconduct by staff in children's homes
cases.who: Children's homes (児童養護施設) in Japan
cases.what: A Yomiuri Shimbun survey published in December 2021 found that in the five years to fiscal 2020 at least 47 staff at children's homes across Japan were confirmed to have committed indecent acts against children in their care, and that 69 children were victims. Only a summary of the survey was accessible; the full article was withdrawn by the provider.

cases.title: Japan — 'JK business' and compensated dating (police survey 2024; US TIP 2025)
cases.who: JK businesses, often with organized-crime ties
cases.what: The 'JK business' sells simulated dates and services with high-school girls. A National Police Agency survey at the end of December 2024 counted 91 establishments advertising in this way, 70 per cent in Tokyo. Kanagawa first regulated it in 2011 and Tokyo enacted a dedicated ordinance in 2017. The 2025 US TIP report says JK variants and 'compensated dating', often tied to organized crime, continue to facilitate sex trafficking of Japanese children and of children from China, South Korea, Laos, the Philippines, Singapore and Vietnam.

networks.name: Johnny & Associates (now Smile-Up)
networks.what: Japan's dominant boy-band talent agency. Its founder Johnny Kitagawa abused boys and young men from the early 1970s to the mid-2010s (independent investigation, 2023); the company admitted it and by Aug 2026 had decided to compensate 585 people.

networks.name: Roman Catholic Church
networks.what: The Holy See governs about 1.3 billion Catholics. From 1922 (and 1962) canonical abuse cases were handled under strict secrecy; from 2001 they were reserved to the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith under pontifical secret, which was lifted in December 2019. National inquiries in Ireland, the US, Australia, Germany, France, the Netherlands, Belgium, Portugal, Spain and elsewhere found bishops moved accused clergy and avoided police. The UN Committee on the Rights of the Child in 2014 found practices that led to impunity.

patterns.pattern: The adoption pipeline that keeps moving
patterns.role: Sending country, later closed or suspended
patterns.role_note: 1,991 children sent abroad 2003–2022 (Selman). 2007: shutdown: Nepal halts all intercountry adoptions (April) after baby-buying reports
patterns.pattern_summary: Intercountry adoption is the adoption of a child from one country by parents in another. From the 1950s onward the children came from a series of countries in turn. South Korea sent about 164,000 children abroad between 1953 and 2008. Later the main sources included Romania in the 1990s, Guatemala until 2008, Cambodia, Vietnam, Nepal and Ethiopia. In each of these, investigations found children who had been bought, taken from their families or falsely registered as orphans, and adoptions were stopped or suspended by the sending country, the receiving countries, or both. In 2025 South Korea's Truth and Reconciliation Commission found the state responsible for human rights violations in its overseas adoptions. Receiving countries also began to investigate: the Netherlands suspended all intercountry adoption in 2021 after a government committee reported abuses, and China ended the practice in 2024. The map draws 59 documented adoption flows and marks which sending countries were later closed or suspended.

patterns.pattern: Officials who took part or looked away
patterns.role_note: Nepal → India — trafficking of girls to Indian brothels (estimates).
patterns.pattern_summary: In 238 cases on this map, police officers, prosecutors, judges, politicians, civil servants, soldiers or intelligence officers took part in the abuse, or a court or inquiry found that they ignored, concealed or obstructed it. In Rotherham, in the north of England, an independent inquiry in 2014 estimated that about 1,400 children had been sexually exploited between 1997 and 2013 and called the failures of the council and the police "blatant"; three earlier reports had been suppressed or ignored. In Australia in 1972, a senior police officer offered a detective a promotion to stop investigating a monsignor. In North Wales, the police investigated allegations against their own officers. In Mexico, after the journalist Lydia Cacho exposed an abuse ring in Cancún, Puebla state police arrested her in 2005, and leaked phone calls recorded the state governor discussing her detention; he was arrested in 2021 on torture charges.

patterns.pattern: Where nobody is counting
patterns.role: No survey data on online abuse in its region
patterns.role_note: Childlight's 2026 update found South Asia lacking representative survey data on technology-facilitated child sexual exploitation.
patterns.pattern_summary: Most counts of child abuse and trafficking come from three sources, and each leaves large parts of the world out. The first is surveys that ask a representative sample of people about their experiences. Childlight, a research centre that combines such surveys into global estimates, had them from only 60 countries in its 2026 update, too few to represent South Asia, West and Central Africa, or the Middle East and North Africa. The second is official statistics that governments send to the UN; its 2024 global report on trafficking covered 156 countries, but only 72 supplied figures for 2023. The third is reports from technology companies to the US CyberTipline; in 2025, 14 percent of its 23.4 million reports could not be assigned to any country, and North Korea had 12, a number that reflects how few people there can use American apps. The research for this map also found no national inquiry into abuse in institutions in Italy, Brazil, the Philippines or India.

cases.title: Nepal → India — trafficking of girls to Indian brothels (estimates)
cases.who: Trafficking networks recruiting via false job, marriage and online romance offers
cases.what: The 2025 US TIP report says traffickers use job offers and online romance scams to recruit Nepali women and children to India for sex trafficking; Nepali courts convicted 406 traffickers (231 for sex trafficking) in the year. A 2024 study it cites found a majority of workers in Nepal's adult entertainment sector were sex-trafficking victims, nearly half of them children. Research collated on Wikipedia gives estimates of 5,000–10,000 Nepali women and girls trafficked to India each year across a 1,850 km open border.
cases.cover_up: US TIP 2025: serious concerns of official complicity; traffickers bribe some Indian officials to fly Nepali workers to third countries.

cases.title: 'Hidden in Plain Sight' — Australian Parliament recognises orphanage trafficking as modern slavery
cases.who: Australian volunteers, donors, schools and tour operators supporting overseas orphanages
cases.what: The Joint Standing Committee's report 'Hidden in Plain Sight', released on 6 December 2017 from its inquiry into establishing a Modern Slavery Act, recognised orphanage trafficking as a form of modern slavery to be covered by the Act. A chapter was devoted to orphanage trafficking, orphanage tourism and Australian donations, with evidence from ReThink Orphanages, Lumos, the ChildSafe campaign and others. Australia's Modern Slavery Act followed in 2018; Lumos supported the change.
cases.network: Orphanage trafficking and orphanage tourism (recruitment of children into institutions for donations)

cases.title: Kolkata red-light areas — rescues of trafficked Nepali girls and minors (2015, 2025)
cases.who: Brothel keepers and traffickers in Kolkata
cases.what: In January 2015 police, with International Justice Mission and three NGOs, freed six young women trafficked from Nepal from four brothels in Kolkata's largest red-light area; all had fake adult ID documents, which IJM said traffickers issue to underage girls. On 10 September 2025 Kolkata Police's Anti-Human Trafficking Unit rescued ten people including nine minor girls from a house in Burtolla, North Kolkata, and arrested six people, including the couple running it (charged). The 2025 US TIP report says traffickers recruit significant numbers of Nepali and Bangladeshi women and girls for sex trafficking in India.

cases.title: Nepal — baby-buying in intercountry adoption; 2007 shutdown
cases.who: Orphanages and adoption intermediaries
cases.what: A Daily Telegraph investigation in March 2007 described baby-buying, bribes and deception of birth families. In April 2007 Nepal's new minister halted all intercountry adoptions, leaving about 400 Western families waiting; about 440 pending cases were processed after November 2007, and new rules were published in May 2008. UNICEF and Terre des hommes published 'Adopting: The Rights of the Child' in August 2008. Wikipedia records that the US later suspended adoptions of children declared abandoned because documents were unreliable.

cases.title: Nepal child care homes — 'paper orphans' and recruitment by agents
cases.who: Child care homes (orphanages) in Nepal, many registered as NGOs; recruiting agents
cases.what: Nepal's National Child Rights Council counted 417 registered child care homes holding 10,905 children in 2021/22, and UNICEF estimates about 85% have a living parent or guardian. Agents take money from rural families with promises of schooling and are paid commissions by institutions; NGOs documented a child admitted on a forged parental death certificate. Researchers say homes use children to attract donations and that many operate unregistered. Only about 200 of 753 local governments had appointed the child welfare officers required by the Act Relating to Children (2018).

cases.title: Kamathipura, Mumbai — red-light district fed by trafficking from Nepal and Indian states
cases.who: Brothels of Kamathipura
cases.what: Kamathipura, Mumbai's oldest and largest red-light district and one of Asia's largest, was established over 150 years ago under British rule; the BBC in 2013 put its sex workers at an estimated 20,000. Girls were trafficked there from poor villages in other Indian states, some as young as 11, on promises of domestic work. The 2025 US Trafficking in Persons report is cited, though it could not be opened for this map, for a shift of sex trafficking in India toward spas, hotels and private residences, and for 2022 crime-data figures of 204 convicted traffickers and 1,134 acquittals; that report could not be opened in this pass (state.gov blocked).

flows.what: Large numbers of Nepalese women and girls trafficked into Kamathipura in recent decades.

flows.title: Canada → Nepal (aid-worker offender)
flows.what: A Canadian humanitarian working with street children abused boys at his home in Nepal.

networks.name: Orphanage trafficking and orphanage tourism (recruitment of children into institutions for donations)
networks.what: A recurring pattern in which orphanages are set up or kept full to attract foreign donations, volunteers and tourists, recruiting children who mostly have living parents, sometimes with payments to families or forged documents. Governments and the US State Department have recognised it as trafficking, and Australia's parliament classed it as modern slavery in 2017.

patterns.pattern: Peacekeepers and aid workers in crisis zones
patterns.role: Mission or crisis zone where children were abused
patterns.role_note: ONUMOZ Mozambique — soldiers recruited girls aged 12–18 into prostitution (Machel study).
patterns.pattern_summary: In war zones and refugee camps, children have been sexually abused by soldiers and aid workers sent to protect them or to provide food and shelter. In 2002 a report by the UN refugee agency and Save the Children described aid workers and peacekeepers in Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone trading food and other aid for sex with children. In Haiti, a UN investigation found that Sri Lankan peacekeepers had abused at least nine children between 2004 and 2007, and 114 soldiers were sent home; none was jailed in Sri Lanka. In the Central African Republic, children reported abuse by French soldiers and UN troops in 2014 and 2015; French judges closed the case against the French soldiers in 2018 without charges. An independent commission found 83 alleged perpetrators among people working on the World Health Organization's Ebola response in the Democratic Republic of the Congo between 2018 and 2020, 21 of them WHO staff, and victims as young as 13. patterns.pattern: War and the taking of children
patterns.role: Abductions and sexual violence by armed groups

The UN verifies and publishes these attacks country by country each year.

cases.who: UN Operation in Mozambique (ONUMOZ) soldiers
cases.what: The UN study 'Impact of Armed Conflict on Children' led by Graça Machel (August 1996) found that after the 1992 peace treaty, ONUMOZ soldiers recruited girls aged 12 to 18 into prostitution. cases.title: Mozambique, Cabo Delgado — abduction of children by ISIS-linked armed groups
cases.who: Islamic State–Mozambique Province ('Al-Shabaab' locally) and other armed groups; also Mozambique defence forces (sexual violence, 2023)
cases.what: The UN verified the abduction of 468 children (371 boys, 97 girls) by armed groups in Cabo Delgado in 2024, 392 for recruitment, and sexual violence against 5 girls. In 2023 it verified 92 abductions (4 for sexual violence) and sexual violence against 12 girls attributed to the Mozambique Defence Armed Forces (5), armed groups (4) and the police Rapid Intervention Unit (3).

cases.title: Bishop Carlos Ximenes Belo — Vatican sanctions
cases.who: Salesians; Bishop Carlos Filipe Ximenes Belo (Nobel Peace laureate)
cases.what: On 28 September 2022 Dutch magazine De Groene Amsterdammer reported that two men said Bishop Belo had abused them and other boys in Fatumaca and Dili, before and during his time as bishop. The next day the Vatican confirmed it had received allegations in 2019 and imposed disciplinary sanctions in 2020: limits on movement and ministry, no contact with minors and no contact with Timor-Leste. The sanctions were reinforced in 2021. Belo had left Timor in 2002 and worked in Maputo, Mozambique from 2004.
cases.cover_up: Vatican received allegations in 2019 and imposed sanctions in 2020 but did not disclose them until a magazine reported the case in 2022

cases.title: Mozambique — girls exploited along the Maputo–South Africa highway and at mines (US TIP 2025)
cases.who: Traffickers at rest stops, bars, mining areas; non-state armed groups
cases.what: The 2025 US TIP report says traffickers exploit girls in rest stops, bars and restaurants along the Maputo–South Africa highway and around mines, and that non-state armed groups abducted children and sexually exploited girls. Girls as young as 11 working as nannies are vulnerable when employment ends.

networks.name: UN peacekeeping operations (Department of Peace Operations)
networks.what: UN Secretary-General reports record 357 SEA allegations against peacekeeping personnel in 2006, falling to 51 in 2014 and rising to 102 in 2024. In 2024, 27 of 125 identified victims were children. Most allegations since 2018 come from MONUSCO (DRC) and MINUSCA (CAR). Criminal accountability rests with troop-contributing countries; the UN can only repatriate.

networks.name: Islamic State (ISIS / Da'esh)
networks.what: ISIS abducted thousands of Yazidi women and children from Sinjar in August 2014 and ran markets for their sale; the UN COI found genocide. Affiliates in West Africa, the Sahel and Mozambique are verified by the UN as abducting children.

networks.what: Order present in more than 130 countries. Documented cases include Boys' Town Sydney, the Don Rua juvenate in the Netherlands, US schools, Julian Fox (moved from Australia to Fiji in 1999), and Vatican sanctions on Salesian Bishop Belo of Timor-Leste.

patterns.pattern: Governments that took children
patterns.role_note: Nazi Germany — kidnapping of Polish and other children for Germanization (RuSHA trial) (receiving or involved).
patterns.pattern_summary: Some of the largest removals of children from their families were carried out by governments as a matter of policy. During Argentina's military dictatorship from 1976 to 1983, about 500 babies were taken from mothers held in detention and given to other families; in 2012 a court found this had been a "systematic plan", and by July 2025, 140 of those children had been identified. Under Franco's dictatorship in Spain, children were taken from Republican mothers and later from unmarried mothers. Canada, Australia and the United States removed Indigenous children from their families and placed them in residential schools or with non-Indigenous families. In 1951 Denmark sent a group of Greenlandic children to live with Danish families, and France moved children from the island of Réunion to rural France. Since 2022 Russia has deported children from occupied parts of Ukraine; in March 2023 the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for President Vladimir Putin and Maria Lvova-Belova over these deportations.

cases.title: Nazi Germany — kidnapping of Polish and other children for Germanization (RuSHA trial)
cases.who: SS Race and Settlement Main Office (RuSHA), Lebensborn e.V., SS
cases.what: Nazi Germany seized children judged 'racially valuable' in occupied Poland and elsewhere, held them in Lebensborn and other homes and placed them with German families under new identities; DW reports estimates of up to 200,000 Polish children kidnapped and forcibly 'Germanized'. In the RuSHA trial (United States v. Ulrich Greifelt et al., Nuremberg Military Tribunal I), 14 leading officials of the SS Race and Settlement Main Office, Lebensborn and related bodies were charged with crimes including the kidnapping of 'racially valuable' children; charges were read on 10 October 1947, the trial ran from 20 October 1947 to 17 February 1948, and on 10 March 1948 the tribunal convicted 13 — Greifelt was sentenced to life — and acquitted one.
cases.network: SS Race and Settlement Main Office (RuSHA) and Lebensborn e.V.

cases.title: Serbia — 'Torment not Treatment' investigation of institutions for children and adults with disabilities
cases.who: Serbian state institutions for people with mental disabilities
cases.what: Mental Disability Rights International's four-year investigation, released on 14 November 2007, covered conditions affecting more than 17,000 people with disabilities in Serbian institutions. It found children and adults tied to beds or kept in cribs for years, filthy conditions, contagious disease and no oversight, treatment it said was 'tantamount to torture'. It warned of a danger of sexual exploitation: at Vršac men and women lived in mixed wards and staff said they made no effort to determine whether sex was consensual.
cases.cover_up: In 2006 the director of one institution refused to let investigators see a locked area and asked them to leave; Serbian officials called the allegations 'dark propaganda'.

cases.title: Kosovo — trafficking for forced prostitution and the international presence (Amnesty 2004)
cases.who: Criminal networks; demand from NATO KFOR soldiers, UN police and international staff
cases.what: Amnesty International's May 2004 report said Kosovo had become a major destination for women and girls trafficked for forced prostitution since NATO troops and UN administrators arrived in 1999, with the international presence generating 80% of traffickers' income at the time. Women and girls were brought mainly from Moldova, Romania, Ukraine and Russia via Serbia, and local girls were also abducted. The UN peacekeeping department acknowledged in 2004 that peacekeepers had 'come to be seen as part of the problem in trafficking rather than the solution'.
cases.cover_up: Amnesty found no evidence of criminal proceedings against any military personnel in their home countries.

cases.title: Dreamboard / Operation Delego
cases.who: Dreamboard (invitation-only bulletin board, about 600 members)
cases.what: An invitation-only bulletin board, used by an estimated 600 people, whose applicants had to upload abuse material of children aged 12 or under and keep uploading to stay. NBC reported the computers hosting the site were in Georgia, US, and the top administrators were in France and Canada. In August 2011 Attorney General Eric Holder and DHS Secretary Janet Napolitano announced charges against 72 people, with arrests on five continents including 43 in the US. By January 2013, 57 had been arrested, 45 had pleaded guilty and one was convicted at trial; 42 had been sentenced to between 10 years and life. Fifteen were known only by online identities. DOJ said at least 38 children were being abused by group members.

cases.title: Kidflix / Operation Stream
cases.who: Kidflix (paid streaming platform, 1.8 million users 2022–2025)
cases.what: Kidflix, created in 2021, let users stream as well as download abuse videos, paying in cryptocurrency converted to tokens; 91,000 unique videos (6,288 hours) were uploaded. German and Dutch authorities seized the server on 11 March 2025, when it held about 72,000 videos. Operation Stream, led by Bavarian police with 38 countries and Europol, identified 1,393 suspects and arrested 79 during action weeks in March 2025; Europol called it the largest child sexual exploitation operation in its history.

networks.name: SS Race and Settlement Main Office (RuSHA) and Lebensborn e.V.
networks.what: RuSHA racially screened children in occupied territories and Lebensborn ran camps and homes from which selected children were placed with German families under new identities. The Nuremberg RuSHA trial (1947–48) ruled the kidnapping and Germanization of children part of genocide.

cases.title: Trokosi — ritual servitude of girls at shrines
cases.who: Traditional shrines (Ewe in Ghana and Togo; Fon in Benin)
cases.what: Under trokosi, shrines take girls, usually young virgins, as atonement for a relative's alleged wrongdoing; they serve priests without pay, and in most shrines sexual service to the priest is treated as a duty, which defenders deny. cases.title: Nigeria — Kaduna 'Islamic school' raid frees 300+ boys and men

cases.title: T.B. Joshua (SCOAN) — BBC investigation into abuse of disciples

patterns.pattern_summary: Intercountry adoption is the adoption of a child from one country by parents in another. From the 1950s onward the children came from a series of countries in turn.
